lessons.title: -कर / देखकर / करके (-kar / dekhkar / karke) — chaining actions in sequence
lessons.gloss: having done / having looked / having done — suffix / regular example / irregular example

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Say the जब … तब frame. Two clauses, two verbs, a word at each end. That is a lot of scaffolding for first this, then that — and Hindi has a much shorter way that it uses far more often.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: put -कर on the stem and the clause disappears

segments.text: मैं किताब देखकर आता हूँ. — maiṁ kitāb dekhkar ātā hūṁ. — I look at the book and come. (Literally: having looked, I come.)
The move is the same shape as सकना: take the -ना off the first verb and put -कर on the bare stem.
करना becomes करके — having done (this one is irregular, and it is the commonest of all).

What you get is not a second clause. It is one clause with a chained action inside it, and only the LAST verb takes a person ending. That is why Hindi reaches for it constantly: a speaker can string three actions together and conjugate once.
The order is the order of events. देखकर आता हूँ is look-then-come, never the other way round, so you say the actions in the sequence they happen.

The ending is the verb करना frozen solid. Having looked is literally look-do. Marathi does the same job with its own -ūn; both languages inherited the construction from Sanskrit and each reinforced it with its own material.

segments.instruction: देखना (dekhnā) becomes देखकर (dekhkar), then करना (karnā) becomes करके (karke)
मैं किताब देखकर आता हूँ (maiṁ kitāb dekhkar ātā hūṁ)
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **मैं किताब देखकर आता हूँ** (*maiṁ kitāb dekhkar ātā hūṁ*)]

segments.instruction: which of the two verbs carries the person ending — the last one
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which of the two verbs carries the person ending — **the last one**]

segments.prompt: Chain two actions: look at the book, then come.

feedback.correct: Stem plus -kar, and only the last verb takes the ending.
feedback.incorrect: Strip -nā off dekhnā and add -kar; leave ātā hūṁ to carry the person.

segments.text: What does -कर attach to? (The bare stem, after the -ना comes off.) How many verbs in a -कर sentence take a person ending? (One — the last.)

lessons.title: One clause or two
lessons.gloss: two clauses or one, and how to choose

segments.text: You now have three ways to put two actions in one sentence: aur between two clauses, the जब … तब frame, and -कर inside a single clause. Only one of them conjugates just once.

segments.instruction: maiṁ kitāb dekhtā hūṁ aur ātā hūṁ — two endings
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *maiṁ kitāb dekhtā hūṁ aur ātā hūṁ* — two endings]

segments.instruction: maiṁ kitāb dekhkar ātā hūṁ — one ending
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *maiṁ kitāb dekhkar ātā hūṁ* — one ending]

segments.instruction: which of the two a Hindi speaker says more often — the -कर one
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which of the two a Hindi speaker says more often — **the -कर one**]

segments.prompt: Say the same two actions twice: joined with aur, then chained with -kar.
acceptedResponses: maiṁ kitāb dekhtā hūṁ aur ātā hūṁ; maiṁ kitāb dekhkar ātā hūṁ

feedback.correct: Two endings with aur, one with -kar.
feedback.incorrect: With -kar the first verb keeps no ending at all.

segments.text: How many person endings does a -कर sentence carry? (One.) And an aur sentence with two verbs? (Two.) Then stop.
